title: AI in Healthcare: What Every Woman Needs to Know Now
guestBio: Dr. Maria Ines "Mari" Mitrani is a physician-scientist specializing in regenerative and preventive medicine, with deep expertise in stem cells, women's health, and translating complex science into practical, actionable solutions. She recently completed a certification in AI in healthcare from Harvard Medical School and has co-founded multiple biotech companies spanning stem cells, exosomes, genetic testing, and metabolic health. Dr. Mari was recognized by IFAH as one of the Top 100 Healthcare Leaders and is a fierce advocate for getting more women into the rooms where medical futures are being designed.
excerpt: Dr. Mari Mitrani just completed her AI in healthcare certification from Harvard Medical School — and she's here to give you the honest, unfiltered answer to the question everyone is asking. AI is already reshaping medicine, fertility research, and longevity science, and the women who get in the room now will help decide who gets included. This conversation will change how you think about your health and your future.
metaDescription: Dr. Mari Mitrani answers honestly: will AI replace your doctor? Learn what's changing in medicine, why women must lead it, and how to protect your health now.
keyTakeaways: AI is a powerful tool in medicine, but the human relationship at the heart of healthcare is something no machine can replicate — and that distinction matters for how you advocate for yourself.
We are all beginners when it comes to AI, which means you are not behind — you are exactly on time, and your perspective as a woman belongs in this conversation.
You do not need to know how to code to participate in building the future of healthcare; you need to know what problems to solve and what questions to ask.
Precision medicine is already here, and the most urgent equity question is no longer just who gets treated — it is who gets included when the algorithms are being built.
If a doctor is dismissing what you are telling them about your own body, that is not a dead end — it is a signal to track your symptoms, advocate louder, and change providers if you need to.
Muscle and bone density are longevity investments, and women should be screening and protecting both decades earlier than the current standard of care recommends.
Simple, unglamorous daily habits — sleep, movement, nutrition, stress management — still outperform expensive biohacks, and no amount of technology changes that foundation.

pullQuotes.text: We are all beginners with this technology. You are not behind. Get in before the room fills up without us.
AI will never do the human part of medicine. That is the part that matters.
The bias problem isn't just in the past — it's being baked into the algorithms right now. Who's in the room when that happens?
Your muscle and your bone are not vanity metrics. They are your longevity portfolio. Start investing early.
If your doctor is dismissing you, that is data too. Track everything. Advocate louder. And if you have to — walk out the door.

content:
Let's start with the question you actually came here to ask: Will AI replace your doctor? Dr. Mari Mitrani — physician-scientist, biotech founder, and the woman who just walked out of a Harvard Medical School AI certification program — has the honest answer. And it is more nuanced, more urgent, and more hopeful than anything the headlines are giving you.

This is Part II of Aimee's conversation with Dr. Mari, and if Part I about perimenopause symptoms left you feeling seen, this one is going to leave you feeling activated. Because the future of medicine is being built right now — and the question is not whether you'll be affected. It is whether you'll have a seat at the table while it happens.

AI Has Been in Medicine Longer Than You Think

One of the most grounding things Dr. Mari shares early in this conversation is that AI is not new to healthcare. Algorithms have been quietly working in radiology, pathology, and diagnostics for years. What changed dramatically in the last two years is the accessibility of the technology — and the speed at which it is now evolving. Think of it the way electricity transformed industry: it didn't replace what humans were doing, it radically changed how fast and how well they could do it.

Right now, AI can read a scan faster than the human eye, flag anomalies a radiologist might not catch on a long shift, and process drug discovery data in a fraction of the time it once took research teams years to compile. But a human still signs off. That is not a formality — it is the law, and according to Dr. Mari, it is also the right call. The technology surfaces patterns. The physician brings context, relationship, and judgment. Those are not the same thing.

The Part a Machine Will Never Do

When Aimee presses her for the honest answer — the thing AI genuinely cannot do — Dr. Mari does not hesitate. The human part. Medicine at its best is a relationship. It is a provider who notices that something in your voice is off today. It is the moment you feel heard enough to finally say the thing you've been afraid to say. It is trust built over time. No algorithm, no matter how sophisticated, replicates that. And when we lose sight of that, we lose something essential about what healing actually requires.

That said, Dr. Mari is not here to romanticize a system that has consistently failed women. She is here to tell you that precision medicine — care that is designed around your specific biology, your specific data, your specific life — is no longer a futuristic concept. It is already here. And the most urgent equity question is no longer just who gets treated. It is who gets included when the systems doing the treating are being designed.

The Research Gap — and Why AI Could Close It

For decades, women were excluded from clinical trials. The default human body in medical research was male. The result? Drugs dosed wrong. Symptoms missed. Conditions dismissed. The cardiovascular presentation of a heart attack in a woman still gets overlooked in emergency rooms because the data that trained generations of doctors was built on men.

Dr. Mari is direct about this: the bias problem is not just historical — it is being baked into new algorithms right now. If the data sets used to train AI systems are drawn from research that excluded women, the AI inherits that exclusion. This is why she issues a challenge that landed hard in this episode: women need to get into the rooms where these systems are being designed. Not eventually. Now. Before the room fills up without them.

The good news is that AI also holds real promise for closing the gap. In fertility research alone, machine learning is already being used to evaluate embryo viability in ways that reduce the margin of human subjectivity. Women's hormonal patterns, reproductive timelines, and metabolic profiles — long dismissed as "too complex" to study — are exactly the kind of rich, multivariable data that AI is built to handle.

You Don't Need to Code. You Need to Know What to Ask.

If you just felt a small wave of "this is not for me" — Dr. Mari saw you coming. She addresses it head-on. You do not need a computer science degree. You do not need to understand machine learning architecture. What you need is to understand the problem you are trying to solve, and to have the courage to say: I belong in this conversation.

The women who will shape healthcare AI are not just the ones who can build the tools. They are the clinicians, the advocates, the patients, the founders, and the executives who insist that the tools being built reflect the full reality of human health — including half the population that has historically been left out of it.

Longevity Is Not Just for the Bros

There is an entire ecosystem of longevity content online, and a significant portion of it is built around the bodies, the bloodwork, and the risk profiles of men. Dr. Mari has thoughts about this — warm, pointed, and entirely quotable thoughts. The longevity conversation women need is different. It centers muscle. It centers bone density. It centers the hormonal shifts of perimenopause and menopause as pivotal longevity events, not just inconvenient symptoms to manage.

She wants women screened for bone density and muscle mass decades before the standard of care currently recommends. Because by the time the conventional system flags a problem, you have already lost years of opportunity to protect yourself. And the interventions are not exotic — they are resistance training, protein intake, sleep, and stress management. Unglamorous. Effective. Available to you right now, before any algorithm touches your data.

When Your Doctor Dismisses You

This section of the conversation hit differently. If you have ever sat in an exam room and been told your symptoms are stress, or anxiety, or just part of being a woman — this one is for you. Dr. Mari's advice is both validating and activating: track everything. Date it. Describe it. Bring it in writing. And if you are consistently dismissed by a provider who will not engage with what you are telling them about your own body, that is not a reflection of your credibility. That is a signal to find a provider who will actually listen.

You are the expert on your own experience. The medical system, at its best, is your partner in decoding it. You deserve that partnership — and you are allowed to keep looking until you find it.

The Bottom Line

AI will not replace your doctor. But it will change what medicine looks like — what gets caught, what gets treated, who gets included, and who gets left behind. The women who understand that now, who get curious now, who raise their hands now, are the ones who will help determine which future we actually get. Dr. Mari's message is clear: we are all beginners. You are not late. You are exactly on time. Get in the room.]]>
